Mowing lawns as a tick control intervention has received limited attention, but in the few studies that have investigated this intervention, no impact has been observed on tick densities. The first paper examines the effect in residential lawns, while the second is focused on hiking trails. The main issue appears to be that tick densities are generally low in lawns, so it is hard to detect a significant effect. Lerman, S. B., & D’Amico, V. (2019). Lawn mowing frequency in suburban areas has no detectable effect on Borrelia spp. vector Ixodes scapularis (Acari: Ixodidae). PLoS One, 14(4), e0214615. Lee, X., Maxson, G. A., & Paskewitz, S. (2023). Single mowing event does not reduce abundance of Ixodes scapularis (Acari: Ixodidae) and Dermacentor variabilis (Acari: Ixodidae) on recreational hiking trails. Journal of Medical Entomology, 60(1), 228-234.

Removal of understory vegetation has been shown to reduce tick densities by ~ 50% in some cases, although this might depend on the type of understory as much of this work has been focused on Japanese barberry, which forms a very thick understory. Williams, S. C., & Ward, J. S. (2010). Effects of Japanese barberry (Ranunculales: Berberidaceae) removal and resulting microclimatic changes on Ixodes scapularis (Acari: Ixodidae) abundances in Connecticut, USA. Environmental entomology, 39(6), 1911-1921.
I do not believe that a mulch or gravel barrier will significantly impact tick densities  but rather may act as a barrier between edge habitat and lawns to reduce contact rates.

Litter removal and accumulation have been shown to impact tick densities and litter removal has been shown to impact tick survival in microcosms. Litter removal has mostly been tested in forested landscapes, rather than in edge habitat. I think there may be less of an impact on tick densities when removing leaf litter when understory is present, where it can provide additional protective effects. Schulze, T. L., Jordan, R. A., & Hung, R. W. (1995). Suppression of subadult Ixodes scapularis (Acari: Ixodidae) following removal of leaf litter. Journal of medical entomology, 32(5), 730-733. Jordan, R. A., & Schulze, T. L. (2020). Artificial accumulation of leaf litter in forest edges on residential properties via leaf blowing is associated with increased numbers of host-seeking Ixodes scapularis (Acari: Ixodidae) nymphs. Journal of medical entomology, 57(4), 1193-1198. Linske, M. A., Stafford III, K. C., Williams, S. C., Lubelczyk, C. B., Welch, M., & Henderson, E. F. (2019). Impacts of deciduous leaf litter and snow presence on nymphal Ixodes scapularis (Acari: Ixodidae) overwintering survival in coastal New England, USA. Insects, 10(8), 227. Burtis, J. C., & Pflueger, C. (2017). Interactions between soil?dwelling arthropod predators and Ixodes scapularis under laboratory and field conditions. Ecosphere, 8(8), e01914.
I think this intervention will be very effective. Surveys of ticks in lawns have found very low densities relative to forested or edge habitat.

Synthetic spray acaricides have been well-tested and shown to be fairly effective in suppressing ticks. The amount of suppression can vary depending on the application, but I am confident that a relatively high level of suppression would be achieved. This paper is missing some newer study, but is a great overview: Eisen, L., & Dolan, M. C. (2016). Evidence for personal protective measures to reduce human contact with blacklegged ticks and for environmentally based control methods to suppress host-seeking blacklegged ticks and reduce infection with Lyme disease spirochetes in tick vectors and rodent reservoirs. Journal of medical entomology, 53(5), 1063-1092.

Natural (25(b) exempt) acaricides have been show to have limited impact on tick densities or survival in trials. There is also enormous variation between products, making it difficult to expect any consistent suppression. Eisen, L. (2024). Efficacy of unregulated minimum risk products to kill and repel ticks. Emerging Infectious Diseases, 30(1), 1. Dyer, M. C., Requintina, M. D., Berger, K. A., Puggioni, G., & Mather, T. N. (2021). Evaluating the effects of minimal risk natural products for control of the tick, Ixodes scapularis (Acari: Ixodidae). Journal of medical entomology, 58(1), 390-397.
Similar to sprays, granular applications have been show to be highly effective in controlling ticks.

Bait boxes have shown high efficacy in some studies and low in others. The bait uptake by mice seems variable depending somewhat on the ecology of the area. This makes it difficult to provide an estimate for the level of tick suppression expected. Schulze, T. L., Jordan, R. A., Williams, M., & Dolan, M. C. (2017). Evaluation of the SELECT tick control system (TCS), a host-targeted bait box, to reduce exposure to Ixodes scapularis (Acari: Ixodidae) in a Lyme disease endemic area of New Jersey. Journal of medical entomology, 54(4), 1019-1024. Dolan, M. C., Maupin, G. O., Schneider, B. S., Denatale, C., Hamon, N., Cole, C., ... & Stafford, K. C. (2004). Control of immature Ixodes scapularis (Acari: Ixodidae) on rodent reservoirs of Borrelia burgdorferi in a residential community of southeastern Connecticut. Journal of medical entomology, 41(6), 1043-1054. Machtinger, E. T., & Li, A. Y. (2019). Tick control bait box use by Peromyscus spp. influenced by habitat placement but raises questions on disease ecology. Ecosphere, 10(12), e02972.

As with bait boxes, results vary somewhat with tick tubes, but there has been less study of this method. Again efficacy seems to be dependent on the ecology of the deployment location, but without better data, I am not particularly confident in my estimates. Green, K. D., Tiffin, H. S., Brown, J. Journal of medical entomology, 61(6), 1459-1469. Brown, J. E., Miller, T. M., & Machtinger, E. T. (2020). Tick tubes reduce blacklegged tick burdens on white?footed mice in Pennsylvania, USA. Integrated tick management in south central Wisconsin: impact of invasive vegetation removal and host-targeted acaricides on the density of questing Ixodes scapularis (Acari: Ixodidae) nymphs. Journal of Medical Entomology, 58(6), 2358-2367.

There is limited study on the effect of bird feeders on ticks. I would imagine food would attract hosts to that location, and ticks might drop off, but how strong the impact would be is hard to estimate.

The effect of deer fencing on tick densities is somewhat variable in the literature. I would expect some effect, but it will depend largely on the size of the area fenced and whether there are alternative hosts available that can move tick through the fence, which is why I am not particularly confident in my estimates here. If used appropriately, synthetic repellents are very effective in avoiding ticks. The main issue appears to be that people do not use them. Beck, A., Bjork, J., Biggerstaff, B. J., Eisen, L., Eisen, R., Foster, E., ... & Hinckley, A. F. (2022). Knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors regarding tick-borne disease prevention in Lyme disease-endemic areas of the Upper Midwest, United States. Ticks and tick-borne diseases, 13(3), 101925.

Natural repellents have shown limited and highly variable efficacy and what is more those that do work appear to wear off quickly. They may have some small protective effect, but are unlikely to provide long lasting protection against tick bites. Eisen, L. (2024). Efficacy of unregulated minimum risk products to kill and repel ticks. Emerging Infectious Diseases, 30(1), 1. Burtis, J. C., Ford, S. L., Parise, C. M., Eisen, R. J., & Eisen, L. (2024). If anything, I would expect a environmental benefit from removing people from edge habitat and forested areas.
